name: OpenCV
baseline: ImageMagick (6.8.9-9 and 6.9.7-4 in pillow-perf; 7.1.1 in the libvips Speed-and-memory-use benchmark)
workload: pillow-perf: resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image (bilinear/bicubic), Gaussian blur and a load/transpose/resize/blur cycle; libvips wiki: crop, 10 percent bilinear shrink and 3x3 sharpen of a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF.
claimed_speedup: pillow-perf on Core i5-4430 (derived from page data): bicubic 2560x1600 to 320x200 takes 5.41 ms for OpenCV 4.1.2 vs 89.2 ms for ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 (16.5x); to 2048x1280 48.2 vs 222.93 ms (4.6x); to 5478x3424 bicubic 115.25 vs 1256.13 ms (10.9x) and bilinear 57.74 vs 1007.63 ms (17.5x); Gaussian blur radius 1 px 69.39 vs 675.34 ms (9.7x), 10 px 445.67 vs 1768.07 ms (4.0x), 30 px 1399.39 vs 4090.08 ms (2.9x). libvips wiki: whole pipeline 3.15 s for opencv 4.10 vs 4.41 s for magick 7.1.1 (1.4x, derived from page data). speedtest-resize (Core i7 3.4GHz, JPEG load, 150x100 thumbnail, save; via go-opencv): 0.110 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (5.2x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: pillow-perf uses the opencv-python binary wheel (OpenCV 4.1.2 in the results); the libvips wiki used the Ubuntu package (opencv 4.10).
hardware: pillow-perf: Intel Core i5-4430 @ 3.00GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.3 (also Xeon 8124M, EPYC 7571 and Core i5-8279U files in the same directory). libvips wiki: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04.
tradeoffs: Large dependency; BGR channel order; cv::resize with bilinear or bicubic does not apply an anti-aliasing filter on strong downscales (per the pillow-resize README), so output differs from convolution-based resamplers such as Pillow, libvips or ImageMagick; JPEG load is slower than ImageMagick in pillow-perf (47.89 vs 27.38 ms on the i5-4430).
caveats: Baseline versions are old (ImageMagick 6.x) in pillow-perf, and the suite is maintained by the Pillow and Pillow-SIMD authors. OpenCV bilinear and Lanczos3 cells are empty for the 320x200 and 2048x1280 targets; the Lanczos row for 5478x3424 is OpenCV Lanczos4 (439.03 ms) against ImageMagick Lanczos3 (1495.61 ms), so not like for like. The libvips pipeline is I/O dominated and the wiki itself says the test flatters libvips; OpenCV does not thread automatically there. vips-bench issue 8 points out that the benchmark programs use different resampling algorithms (affine bilinear in libvips, convolution resampling in Pillow, ImageMagick and others), so the pipelines are not strictly equivalent.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use table (raw wiki page), pillow-perf result data docs/src/data/*.json and the speedtest-resize README, all reached from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: Skia
workload: pillow-perf: resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image to 320x200 and 2048x1280 with bilinear and Lanczos filters (Skia 53, SSE2).
claimed_speedup: Xeon E5-2666 v3 (c4.large): 2560x1600 to 320x200 Lanczos 18.1 ms for Skia vs 127.67 ms for ImageMagick (7.1x, derived from page data); bilinear 6.41 vs 46.15 ms (7.2x); to 2048x1280 Lanczos 39.8 vs 276.76 ms (7.0x). Core i5-4258U: Lanczos 320x200 24.8 vs 156.8 ms (6.3x).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2666 v3 @ 2.90GHz on Amazon EC2 c4.large, Ubuntu 16.04.1 (macbook.json: Intel Core i5-4258U @ 2.40GHz)
stars_or_usage: 11k stars (GitHub mirror of skia.googlesource.com); used in Chrome and Android
tradeoffs: Graphics library, not an image-processing toolbox; heavy build; the resize path measured is one SkBitmap scale call among many APIs.
caveats: Skia 53 dates from 2016 and the suite is maintained by the Pillow-SIMD authors, who report Pillow-SIMD faster than Skia (3.4 AVX2 Lanczos 320x200 7.38 ms vs Skia 18.1 ms on the same machine). Only the c4.large and macbook files include Skia; modern Skia may differ.
found_via: pillow-perf result data docs/src/data/c4.large.json and macbook.json (competitor list skia-53), reached from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: Pillow
workload: pillow-perf: resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image, RGB to L conversion, 3D color LUT and Gaussian blur, compared with Pillow 7.0.0.
claimed_speedup: Core i5-4430 (derived from page data): Lanczos 2560x1600 to 320x200 40.46 ms for Pillow 7.0.0 vs 134.41 ms for ImageMagick (3.3x); bilinear 15.83 vs 47.76 ms (3.0x); RGB to L conversion 5.25 vs 51.45 ms (9.8x); 3D LUT with a 4^3 table 111.19 vs 3353.63 ms (30x); blur radius 1 px 185.67 vs 675.34 ms (3.6x), 10 px 187.53 vs 1768.07 ms (9.4x), 30 px 186.41 vs 4090.08 ms (21.9x); JPEG load 21.39 vs 27.38 ms.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4430 @ 3.00GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.3 (same trends on Xeon 8124M, EPYC 7571, Core i5-8279U)
stars_or_usage: 13.9k stars; the standard Python imaging library
tradeoffs: Python-only API (not callable from C++ without embedding CPython); single-threaded; Lanczos resize is convolution-based with proper anti-aliasing.
caveats: The benchmark repository belongs to the python-pillow organisation (first-party, hence tier C), the ImageMagick baseline is the old 6.9.7-4, and Pillow-SIMD is 4 to 6 times faster than plain Pillow in the same files. The libvips Speed-and-memory-use table includes only Pillow-SIMD, not plain Pillow.
found_via: pillow-perf result data docs/src/data/i5-4430.json (competitor pillow-7.0 against imagemagick-6.9).

name: OpenImageIO
workload: libvips benchmark: load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 pixels off every edge, shrink 10 percent with bilinear interpolation, sharpen with a 3x3 convolution, save (oiiotool 2.5.18).
claimed_speedup: 3.46 s for oiio vs 4.41 s for magick and 4.44 s for convert (1.3x, derived from page data); the page's own 'times slower than libvips' column reads oiio 6.07 vs magick 7.74 and convert 7.79.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04 (run 12 Aug 2025)
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars; VFX industry standard (Academy Software Foundation)
tradeoffs: Large dependency set; peak memory 2236.57 MB in this run, higher than ImageMagick (1500.52 MB) and libvips (94.28 MB).
caveats: Modest 1.3x margin on a trivial, I/O-dominated test that the wiki says flatters libvips. The wiki notes the test uses oiiotool, which 'may not be the best way to test the library'. Run by the libvips maintainer, who is the benchmark author (third party for OpenImageIO). vips-bench issue 8 points out that the benchmark programs use different resampling algorithms (affine bilinear in libvips, convolution resampling in Pillow, ImageMagick and others), so the pipelines are not strictly equivalent.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use shootout table (oiio row), from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: FFmpeg (libswscale and filters)
workload: libvips benchmark: load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 pixels off every edge, shrink 10 percent with bilinear interpolation, sharpen with a 3x3 convolution, save (ffmpeg 7.1.1 command line).
claimed_speedup: 2.06 s for ffmpeg vs 4.41 s for magick and 4.44 s for convert (2.1x, derived from page data); the page's own 'times slower than libvips' column reads ffmpeg 3.61 vs magick 7.74.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04 (run 12 Aug 2025)
tradeoffs: The measured tool is the ffmpeg command line, not a lean resize library; peak memory 1338.36 MB. GitHub lists LGPL-2.1 with GPL-2.0 and GPL-3.0 options for some components.
caveats: One trivial I/O-dominated test, with TIFF handling that dominates the time; the benchmark was not designed around swscale. Already recorded entries (zimg, yuv2rgb) use libswscale as their baseline rather than ImageMagick. vips-bench issue 8 points out that the benchmark programs use different resampling algorithms (affine bilinear in libvips, convolution resampling in Pillow, ImageMagick and others), so the pipelines are not strictly equivalent.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use shootout table (ffmpeg row), from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: epeg
workload: speedtest-resize: load a 5616x3744 JPEG photo, scale to a 150x100 thumbnail, write a JPEG; average time per file.
claimed_speedup: Third scenario (Intel Core i7 3.4GHz, Ubuntu 16.10): epeg 0.079 s per file vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (7.2x, derived from page data). The same table lists ImageMagick_thumbnail (with the jpeg:size hint) at 0.057 s, which is faster than epeg.
hardware: Intel Core i7 3.4GHz, Ubuntu 16.10 (scenario run by a contributor, 'nono')
tradeoffs: JPEG only; reduces size by decoding only the DCT coefficients needed (libjpeg scaled decode), so quality is that of DCT-domain scaling rather than a Lanczos or bicubic resample; speedup is proportional to the pixel-count ratio between source and thumbnail.
caveats: The shootout author's own ImageMagick -thumbnail command with a jpeg:size hint beats epeg in the same table, so epeg only beats the plain ImageMagick resize command. The speedtest-resize benchmark is a Go program that drives each tool (the page was read via the repo README, not run). The mattes/epeg repository is a maintained copy of Enlightenment's epeg, not a GitHub fork.
found_via: github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize README (Go image resize shootout comparing ImageMagick, GraphicsMagick, libvips, OpenCV, epeg).

name: Imageflow
workload: Resizing and re-encoding JPEGs through imageflow_tool or libimageflow (README claim; the benchmark page is on imageflow.io).
claimed_speedup: README: imageflow_tool is 'Up to 17x faster than ImageMagick'. A WebSearch snippet of the imageflow.io benchmark page adds 'about 17x faster than ImageMagick and 2-3x faster than libvips for resizing large jpegs' (snippet only).
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 unless a commercial licence is bought; Rust core with a C ABI (four functions needed for bindings), so usable from C++ through that ABI; the repo's recent commits move image codecs to Rust ('zen') crates.
caveats: Snippet only for the benchmark page: www.imageflow.io/benchmarks is blocked in this environment, so methodology, versions and hardware are unconfirmed. The repo's benchmarks folder holds dated codec benchmarks (c-vs-zen-codecs, 2026-04-15, and jpeg-q-ssim2), not a resize shootout against ImageMagick. A recorded independent entry (FastResize) also benchmarks against imageflow 2.0. A libvips issue thread and a sharp issue ask for third-party verification of the 17x figure.
found_via: WebSearch 'imageflow benchmark faster than ImageMagick libvips resize results repository' and the imageflow README.

name: moxcms
workload: ICC profile colour transform of a 1997x1331 image with 8-bit samples: RGB to RGB, LUT-based RGB to RGB, RGBA to RGBA and CMYK to RGBA.
claimed_speedup: Published README of moxcms 0.7.4 (NEON / AVX2 columns): RGB to RGB 2.68 / 4.52 ms vs lcms2 13.1 / 27.73 ms vs qcms 6.47 / 4.59 ms; LUT RGB to RGB 6.03 / 12.43 ms vs lcms2 27.60 / 58.26 ms vs qcms 26.72 / 60.80 ms; RGBA to RGBA 2.96 / 4.83 ms vs lcms2 21.97 / 35.70 ms; CMYK to RGBA 9.74 / 21.65 ms vs lcms2 39.71 / 79.40 ms vs qcms 25.97 / 61.54 ms. Against lcms2 that is 3.7x to 7.4x (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 52 stars; 89M crates.io downloads (crate moxcms, max version 0.9.1)
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no C or C++ API seen in the README); pure Rust, no unsafe C dependency; supports CMYK, LAB, GRAY and display-class profiles.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware model, compiler or flags, and no benchmark code linked. The benchmark table appears in the crates.io README for versions 0.3.0 to 0.7.4 but is absent from the current GitHub README and the 0.9.1 line, so the figures may be stale. A WebSearch snippet quoted slightly different LUT figures (7.18 ms NEON), consistent with another version. A recorded entry (jsColorEngine) benchmarks against lcms2 too.
found_via: WebSearch 'moxcms Rust ICC color management benchmark faster than lcms2 qcms skcms', then the crates.io readme endpoint for moxcms 0.7.4.

name: Lycon
baseline: Pillow (PIL) 4.0.0 and scikit-image 0.12.3; parity with OpenCV 3.2+
workload: Resize of a 16k (15360x8640) RGB image with nearest, bilinear, bicubic, Lanczos and area interpolation, plus JPEG and PNG read and write, averaged over 10 runs.
claimed_speedup: Seconds, Lycon vs PIL: upsample bilinear 0.4852 vs 7.2940 (15x), downsample bilinear 0.0258 vs 1.3122 (51x), downsample bicubic 0.1324 vs 1.8153 (13.7x), downsample Lanczos 0.3317 vs 2.4058 (7.2x); resize speed equals OpenCV (0.0258 vs 0.0257 for downsample bilinear); JPG read 0.3409 vs OpenCV 0.5085 (1.5x) and PIL 1.4081 (4.1x).
hardware: Intel Core i7 (Skylake), Ubuntu 14.04; OpenCV 3.2+ (master a85b4b5), Pillow 4.0.0, skimage 0.12.3, Python 2.7.3
tradeoffs: Small subset of OpenCV's resize derived from OpenCV, with JPEG and PNG I/O and NumPy zero-copy interop; Linux and macOS only; the README says its advantages over OpenCV are minimal if OpenCV is installed.
caveats: First-party, 2017-era results against the old Pillow 4.0.0 (before Pillow-SIMD and the later resize work) and single-threaded OpenCV, with no flags or exact CPU model. The resize speed is the same as OpenCV's because the code is derived from it, so the gain is against Pillow and scikit-image. The repo has a perf/ directory that was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch 'FlatCV C image processing library faster than OpenCV resize benchmark github' surfaced ethereon/lycon.

name: Pillow-SIMD
workload: libvips benchmark pipeline (crop, 10 percent bilinear shrink, 3x3 sharpen on a 10000x10000 TIFF); pillow-perf resize of 2560x1600 RGB, colour conversion, 3D LUT and blur.
claimed_speedup: libvips wiki: pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s vs magick 4.41 s and convert 4.44 s (2.9x, derived from page data) on a 16-core machine although Pillow is single-threaded. pillow-perf on Core i5-4430 (derived from page data): Lanczos 2560x1600 to 320x200 6.09 ms (Pillow SIMD 7.0.0 AVX2) vs ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 134.41 ms (22x) and plain Pillow 7.0.0 40.46 ms; bilinear 2.40 vs 47.76 ms (20x); RGB to L 2.17 vs 51.45 ms (24x); 3D LUT 4^3 table 14.59 vs 3353.63 ms (230x). Xeon E5-2666 v3, Pillow SIMD 3.4.0 AVX2 Lanczos 320x200 7.38 ms vs Skia 53 18.1 ms vs ImageMagick 6.8.9-9 127.67 ms.
compiler_and_flags: pillow-perf labels builds '-msse4' and '-mavx2'; compiler version not stated; libvips wiki used the pip package.
hardware: libvips wiki: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04. pillow-perf: Core i5-4430, Xeon 8124M, EPYC 7571, Core i5-8279U, Xeon E5-2666 v3.
tradeoffs: Python extension only; on AMD EPYC 7571 the AVX2 build is no faster than SSE4 (pillow-perf notes 128-bit execution units).
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project: the libvips table is an independent third-party suite (hardware stated, no flags). pillow-perf is run by the Pillow-SIMD authors, and the ImageMagick versions there are old.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use table and pillow-perf docs/src/data/*.json.

name: libvips
workload: pillow-perf: JPEG load/save and a full load/transpose/resize/blur cycle on a 2560x1600 image; speedtest-resize: load a 5616x3744 JPEG, make a 150x100 thumbnail, save.
claimed_speedup: pillow-perf full cycle on Core i5-4430 (vips 8.9 vs ImageMagick 6.9.7-4, cumulative): 102.14 ms vs 328.75 ms (3.2x, derived from page data); JPEG save 36.21 vs 48.04 ms; JPEG load 25.18 vs 27.38 ms. speedtest-resize, Pentium T2390 scenario: vipsthumbnail 0.120 s vs ImageMagick_resize 2.316 s (19x, derived) and ImageMagick_thumbnail 0.326 s; Core i7 3.4GHz scenario: vipsthumbnail 0.115 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (4.9x, derived), vips 0.070 s, but ImageMagick_thumbnail 0.057 s is faster than vips in that scenario.
hardware: speedtest-resize: Intel Pentium Dual T2390 @ 1.86GHz Ubuntu 14.04, and Intel Core i7 3.4GHz Ubuntu 16.10; pillow-perf: Core i5-4430 @ 3.00GHz Ubuntu 18.04.3
stars_or_usage: 11.7k stars; used by Mastodon, Rails and imgproxy per its README
tradeoffs: Fastest on large images and with JPEG shrink-on-load; for very small PNGs libvips was slower and heavier than ImageMagick in a user report (libvips issue 3654: 0.41 s and 10.6 MB vs 0.10 s and 10 MB for a 500KB PNG to 64x64).
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project. Third-party numbers show the ImageMagick thumbnail mode with a jpeg:size hint matching or beating libvips on one machine. The pillow-perf suite is by the Pillow-SIMD authors. In libvips discussion 4710 (user-run, hardware not captured) libvips took 2.133 s for 100 6000x4000 JPEGs vs GraphicsMagick 2.015 s and ImageMagick 2.325 s, because libjpeg dominates; the maintainer notes the advantage appears on larger images and multi-operation pipelines.
found_via: github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize README, pillow-perf data files, libvips issue 3654 and libvips discussion 4710.

name: GraphicsMagick
baseline: ImageMagick (npm 'imagemagick' CLI wrapper in the sharp benchmark; ImageMagick resize and thumbnail commands in speedtest-resize)
workload: sharp benchmark: decompress a 2725x2225 JPEG, resize to 720x588 with Lanczos 3, compress to JPEG at quality 80; also a 2048x1536 RGBA PNG resized to 720x540 with premultiply and PNG output.
claimed_speedup: sharp docs, ops/sec (derived ratios from page data): AMD64 JPEG gm 21.04 vs imagemagick 16.23 (1.3x), PNG gm 13.35 vs imagemagick 10.37 (1.3x); ARM64 JPEG gm 13.72 vs imagemagick 5.85 (2.3x), PNG gm 9.45 vs imagemagick 4.39 (2.2x). speedtest-resize (Core i7 3.4GHz): GraphicsMagick_thumbnail 0.172 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s, but ImageMagick_thumbnail takes 0.057 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (packaged binaries driven from Node.js 24.15.0 on Ubuntu 25.10).
hardware: AWS EC2 c8a.xlarge (4x AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.xlarge (4x ARM Graviton4)
tradeoffs: Same command-line style as ImageMagick with a smaller feature set; the sharp suite shells out to the gm binary.
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project (see its libvips-wiki entry). The sharp benchmark is run by the sharp author, so it is third party for GraphicsMagick; the speedtest-resize author was surprised that GraphicsMagick was slower than ImageMagick in his scenario, so the sign of the result depends on the ImageMagick command used. In libvips discussion 4710 GraphicsMagick (2.015 s) also beat ImageMagick 6 (2.325 s, 1.15x) on 100 JPEGs.
found_via: sharp performance docs (contenders imagemagick, gm, jimp) and github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize README.

name: babl
workload: Pixel format and colour space conversion (GIMP 2.10 and GEGL pipeline).
claimed_speedup: GIMP 2.10 release notes (snippet only): babl is 'up to 10 times faster than LCMS2 for the cases tested'. Disputed: a Little CMS blog post (snippet only) measured lcms2 3.59 s vs babl 6.36 s on 8-bit samples, i.e. lcms2 about 1.8x faster (derived from snippet).
stars_or_usage: 25 stars (read-only GitHub mirror of gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/babl); used by GIMP and GEGL
tradeoffs: Converts between pixel formats with runtime-optimised fast paths and caching; needs lcms2 for CMYK profiles (per search snippet); the GitHub page is a read-only mirror.
caveats: Snippet only: www.gimp.org release notes and littlecms.com are blocked here, so neither the 10x claim nor the rebuttal could be opened. The only independent measurement found contradicts the claim for 8-bit data. Keep as a flagged, low-confidence entry. The GitHub repo page was opened but carries no README claim.
found_via: WebSearch 'babl faster than lcms2 color conversion GEGL benchmark ICC' (GIMP 2.10 release notes and the Little CMS 'Babl throughput comparative' post).
